extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; statesmen, legislators, and anyone studying character and practical ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A catalogue of Aristotelian evaluative standards for human conduct: what counts as the good life, how virtues are defined and formed, when actions are voluntary or excused, and how practical wisdom and pleasure relate to moral action. Useful for evaluating persons, actions, laws, and institutions in light of virtue ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness (the ultimate end)
rubrics_metrics.description: All human action is directed toward a single end or good — Happiness (welfare, well‑being). Happiness consists in activity (energising) of the soul in accordance with virtue and the full development and exercise of relevant powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is practical (not merely theoretical), presupposes development of capacities, and is influenced by external conditions (length of life, wealth, good luck) though these are subordinate. The highest form of happiness is the contemplative life, but practical virtues are central for most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function argument / human activity in accordance with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The good for man lies in the activity proper to his nature — specifically activity guided by reason; the best life manifests the exercise of rational capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the criterion for excellence: activities that realise human rational capacities count more toward the good life than mere pleasure, honor, or wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of virtues: intellectual vs moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues split into those of intellect (excellences of reason, acquired by study/instruction) and those of character (moral virtues, acquired by habituation/discipline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual virtues are developed by teaching; moral virtues by repeated practice. Both kinds are necessary and interdependent for full moral functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of character by habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is produced by habituation: repeated doing of acts with similar quality fixes natural aptitudes in a direction (toward good or evil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation requires external direction, imitation, and discipline; mere intellectual instruction is insufficient. Right acts become 'second nature' through repetition and lead to choice for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtue as a stable state (not mere feeling or aptitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral virtue is a permanent state of the agent — a steady, self‑imposed obedience to a rule of action in recurrent situations — not merely a mood, emotion, or natural endowment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue involves control and regulation of impulses; it prescribes a rule one accepts for action, producing consistent responses across situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the Mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Right action or feeling is the mean between excess and defect relative to the situation; virtue lies in finding the just amount — neither more nor less — appropriate to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean is situation‑sensitive and determined by practical judgment (intuition) rather than rigid formulae. Each virtue has two contrary vices (excess and deficiency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right acts conform to the right rule and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Right actions conform to the 'right rule' and ultimately to reason; the Greeks held that moral conduct is essentially reasonable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules are general and admit exceptions; they state probabilities, not certainties. Knowledge of the rule and acceptance of it as one's rule are part of moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary acts and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done under coercion or through ignorance of relevant circumstances are involuntary and exempt the agent from responsibility; otherwise acts are voluntary and the agent is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither passion nor ignorance of the right rule necessarily extenuates responsibility. The distinction between mere voluntariness and acts done by deliberate choice (with deliberation) is important for moral assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and choice as markers of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation involves thinking about means to ends; actions done after deliberation (chosen actions) are proper evidence of the agent and are central to moral responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate acts imply that the agent's whole nature consents to the act; they are 'his' in a deep sense and reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical wisdom (phronesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical wisdom is the intellectual virtue that apprehends the right rules of conduct, shows how rules follow from the end, and produces the right rule for novel situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom presupposes a clear conception of the human end and a character formed by moral virtue; it is interdependent with moral virtue and distinguishes genuine wisdom from mere cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between intellectual and moral virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: True practical wisdom and true moral virtue are interdependent; neither is complete without the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral virtue helps produce the correct apprehension of ends; intellectual virtue supplies the rationale and systematisation of rules. Without moral virtue, 'cleverness' may substitute but not equal practical wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of experience in moral understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience (moral experience, the actual possession and exercise of good character) is necessary to truly understand moral principles and apply them profitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot reduce moral conduct to exact axioms; experience tests and grounds the applicability of rules, which remain general and admit exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a civic moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a special goodness of character required of the adult citizen for the due exercise of civic functions; it is produced by habituation and concerns fairness in civic roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes distributive justice (allocation among recipients, limited scope) and corrective justice (legal redress). The treatment aims at precision but is bounded by the civic context of Greek life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of pleasures’ moral value
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity; its value depends on the worth of the activity with which it is conjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasures that accompany higher activities (especially contemplative/philosophic activity) are superior. Pleasure is necessary but not the whole or principal ingredient of the good life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incontinence (weakness of will) and moral failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Incontinence (akrasia) characterises agents who know the good but fail to act upon that knowledge due to overpowering desire; the phenomenon is complex and implicates passion and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle locates the source partly in the nature of bodily desires which contain rational elements; the problematic issue is how knowledge can coexist with repeated failure to act accordingly.
